non_blocking_findings: Overhead guard trade-off is sound on its merits. Measured child CPU is 29-39 ms/line idle and 46-50 ms/line under 12 busy loops on 16 cores (gate 150 ms: about 3-4x headroom). Wall is 34-82 ms/line idle-ish and 180-206 ms/line under stress, so the original wall gate of 50 ms/line would have failed in most of those runs. The guard still catches a real regression: a mutant adding 160 ms of CPU per wrapper call fails overhead-200 (and cpu-busy-sleep). It does not catch a wall-only slowdown below 1 s/line, for example a sleep in the wrapper; wall per line is printed but not gated. Acceptable for an instrument whose cost is the same on both sides of the comparison. The design doc (1c / risk table) still says 50 ms/line; only the plan row was amended, so the design text should be reconciled at landing.

The wall hang guard of 200 s is generous. A wrapper that sleeps 2 s per call (400 s total) is caught only after minutes and leaves orphaned runs if the control is killed; I had to clean those up by hand. Consider a lower guard or a timeout around the case.
suite_profile.sh now writes out/sleeper.pid purely so the control can observe the sleeper. It is harmless (inside --out), but it is a production file for a test hook.
overhead-200 still shows wall above the design's 50 ms/line on this loaded host even before stress (82 ms/line once); this is information only now.

Remaining survivors: none found among the round-1 list. Linux was not exercised for real; dash was simulated in round 1 and the later diff does not touch the portability code except a /proc/loadavg redirect in the load-sampler case.
